t.2.100.1: As Rāma, the knower of dharma, was consoling Bharata, Jābāli, the best of brāhmaṇas, spoke to him these words that departed from dharma.
t.2.100.2: Well now, Rāghava! Let your mind not be so futile, like that of a common man, for you are noble-minded and an ascetic.
t.2.100.3: What man is a kinsman to whom? What is there to be gained by anyone from anyone? For a creature is born alone and perishes alone.
t.2.100.4: Therefore, O Rāma, the man who clings to others, thinking 'this is my mother, this is my father,' should be regarded as one who is mad, for no one truly belongs to anyone.
t.2.100.5: Just as some man, going to another village, might stay somewhere for a while, and, leaving that lodging, would set out again on the following day,
t.2.100.6: Even so, O Kākutstha, for men a father, a mother, a house and wealth are but a temporary dwelling; the good do not cling to them.
t.2.100.8: Have yourself consecrated in prosperous Ayodhyā, for the city, wearing her hair in a single braid, awaits you.
t.2.100.7: O best of men, having abandoned his ancestral kingdom, he ought not to set out upon an evil path, painful, rough, and full of thorns.
t.2.100.9: O son of a king, enjoying royal pleasures of great worth, sport in Ayodhyā as Śakra does in Triviṣṭapa.
t.2.100.10: Daśaratha is nothing to you, and you are nothing to him. The king is one person and you are another; therefore do what is being said to you.
t.2.100.11: That king has gone there, where indeed he was bound to go; this is the course of mortals, but you are afflicting yourself in vain.
t.2.100.12: Whoever are devoted to wealth and righteousness, those I pity, and not the others; for they, having met with suffering here in this world, have gone to destruction after death.
t.2.100.13: "The Aṣṭakā rite is offered to the ancestors and the gods": with this thought these people busy themselves. See the waste of food! For what will a dead man eat?
t.2.100.14: If what is eaten here by one person passes into the body of another, then let one offer a śrāddha for a man who is away on a journey; there would be no need for food for him on the road.
t.2.100.15: For these scriptures were composed by clever men as a means to coax people into giving: 'Sacrifice, give, consecrate yourself, practise austerities, renounce!'
t.2.100.17: Placing before you the judgment of the virtuous, which is a guide for all the world, accept the kingdom, propitiated as you are by Bharata.
t.2.100.16: O wise one, settle your mind firmly on this: that world beyond does not exist. Hold to what is before your eyes, and put behind you what lies beyond perception.
